title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in §17 Euler applied his interpolation method to the sines of an arithmetic progression of arcs nΦ, (n+1)Φ, ... and obtained
Φ·f(n) = Σ_{k≥0} (−1)^k (2n)_k /(k!(n+k)^2) · sin((n+k)Φ),
where f(n) = ∫_0^1 x^n (1−x)^{n−1} dx = B(n+1,n) = Γ(n)Γ(n+1)/Γ(2n+1).

This page studies f and specialises the series.

§18–19 (Cor. 1–2). Euler gives the recurrence f(n+1) = n/(2(2n+1)) · f(n). From the Beta ratio, f(n+1)/f(n) = n(n+1)/((2n+1)(2n+2)), which equals n/(2(2n+1)).
- Values: f(1) = 1/2, f(2) = 1/12, f(3) = 1/60, f(4) = 1/280. All are correct.
- Hence f(n) is elementary for integer n.

§20 (Cor. 3), n = 1/2.
- With x = y², f(1/2) = 2∫ y² dy/√(1−y²).
- The inner integral is ∫ y² dy/√(1−y²) = (1/2)∫ dy/√(1−y²) = π/4.
- So f(1/2) = π/2.
- The recurrence then gives f(3/2) = (1/8)(π/2), f(5/2) = (1/8)(3/16)(π/2), f(7/2) = (1/8)(3/16)(5/24)(π/2).

General rational n = μ/ν.
- With x = y^ν, f = ν∫ y^{μ+ν−1} (1−y^ν)^{μ/ν−1} dy.
- Euler's standard reduction lowers the exponent by ν with factor μ/(μ+μ) = 1/2.
- This gives f(μ/ν) = (ν/2)∫ y^{μ−1} (1−y^ν)^{μ/ν−1} dy. In modern terms this is B(n+1,n) = ½B(n,n).
- Euler notes these integrals cover all kinds of transcendentals.

§21 (Cor. 4). Differentiating the §17 series in Φ gives
f(n) = Σ (−1)^k (2n)_k /(k!(n+k)) · cos((n+k)Φ),
a trigonometric series with non-integer frequencies whose sum does not depend on Φ.
- Euler sets it beside the elementary expansion f(n) = Σ (−1)^k C(n−1,k)/(n+1+k).
- Modern check: the sum is Re ∫_0^{e^{iΦ}} t^{n−1}(1+t)^{−2n} dt.
- Split the path into [0,1] plus the arc of the unit circle. On the arc t^{n−1}(1+t)^{−2n} dt = i(2cos(θ/2))^{−2n} dθ, which is purely imaginary.
- So the real part is ∫_0^1 t^{n−1}(1+t)^{−2n} dt. With t = x/(1−x) this becomes ∫_0^{1/2} x^{n−1}(1−x)^{n−1} dx = B(n,n)/2 = f(n).
- The claim is therefore correct for |Φ| < π, in the Abel sense when the series diverges. Example: n = 1 gives 1 − cosΦ·... i.e. Σ(−1)^k cos((k+1)Φ), Abel-summable to 1/2.

§22 (Scholion 1), n = 1/2.
- The coefficients become 4/(2k+1)², giving πΦ/2 = 4Σ(−1)^k sin((2k+1)Φ/2)/(2k+1)².
- With Φ = 2ω this is πω/4 = sin ω − sin 3ω/9 + sin 5ω/25 − ..., the Fourier series of the triangle wave, valid for |ω| ≤ π/2.
- Dividing by ω and letting ω → 0 gives Leibniz's series π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − ....

Purpose: show that interpolation of a sequence of sines yields Fourier-type expansions whose coefficients carry Beta integrals, and so recover known series.
errors: No convergence or range conditions are stated. The cosine series of §21 converges only for small n (roughly n < 1/2, conditionally). Otherwise it holds only in an Abel/summability sense, and only for |Φ| < π. The §22 sine series holds only for |ω| ≤ π/2.
In §22 the passage ω → 0 after dividing by ω interchanges a limit with an infinite sum without justification. The result (Leibniz series) is nevertheless correct.

Euler says the cosine series 'equals' the binomial-expansion series. Both indeed equal f(n), but he gives no direct reason why the Φ-independent trigonometric sum is constant; it follows only through the interpolation derivation.

missed.claim: Euler obtains, via interpolation, a one-parameter family of trigonometric series with fractional frequencies n+k whose sum is constant in Φ and equals the Beta value B(n+1,n). Read correctly, this is the statement that Re∫_0^{e^{iΦ}} t^{n−1}(1+t)^{−2n}dt is constant on the unit circle. It is a mildly interesting early instance of boundary behaviour of a binomial series on |z| = 1 tied to a Beta integral. It is, however, equivalent to known expansions of (2cos(Φ/2))^{−2n}, so it is unlikely to be new to specialists.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only historical: an example of Euler reaching Abel-summation-type identities on the circle of convergence via interpolation, about 40 years before Abel's binomial paper.

deep.surprise_reason: The material is mostly standard Beta-function facts and known Fourier series. The Φ-independent fractional-frequency cosine series with a Beta sum is a nice, correct but non-rigorous by-product, and it is equivalent to known fractional-power cosine expansions.
transcription_corrections: §20: the '[?]' value is ∫yy dy/√(1−yy) = ½∫dy/√(1−yy) = π/(2·2) = π/4, which is consistent with f(1/2) = π/2.

§21: the coefficients in the image appear to be 2n/(1(n+1)), 2n(2n+1)/(1·2(n+2)), 2n(2n+1)(2n+2)/(1·2·3(n+3)), not n/(1(n+1)), n(n+1)/(1·2(n+2)), .... Termwise differentiation of the §17 series requires the 2n-forms.
§19: f:2 = ½·1/6 etc. in the image matches the transcription; the general relation f:(n+1) = n/(2(2n+1)) f:n is correct.
